wrongpool_sentence: How much the wrong pooling costs in retrieval depends on the model, measured over whole corpora with queries pooled the same wrong way (512 tokens): bge-small read with mean pooling loses almost nothing (SciFact nDCG@10 0.708 instead of 0.713; NFCorpus 0.347 instead of 0.343), while MiniLM-L6 read with CLS pooling drops from 0.654 to 0.597 on SciFact and from 0.310 to 0.289 on NFCorpus. Nothing in the code warns you either way. measured here

e5_sentence: e5-small-v2 (each corpus re-embedded with and without "passage: ", on MPS): with both prefixes 0.688 on SciFact (the MTEB results repository has 0.689) and 0.325 on NFCorpus; with neither, 0.680 and 0.318 (paired 95% interval of the difference: -0.028 to +0.013 and -0.014 to +0.001); with only the query prefix, 0.687 and 0.320. Its card's warning is right in direction but small here: under one nDCG@10 point, and both intervals include zero. measured here

On SciFact the curve climbs to 512 for both models: bge-small gains 3.2 points from 128 to 512, and MiniLM-L6, whose default is 256, scores 0.654 at 512 against 0.645 at 256 (its card: "The sequence length was limited to 128 tokens" in training, and input "longer than 256 word pieces is truncated" by default; it still uses text beyond both). On NFCorpus the limit barely matters past 128 (MiniLM is even slightly lower at 512): likely because the opening of these documents already carries their topic. Measure on your own documents before raising or lowering a limit.

tr_reading:
1. In-domain training helps even at this size: in-batch negatives alone take SciFact from 0.713 to 0.746; every arm's paired interval against the starting model is clear of zero.
  2. Mined hard negatives add about one point: BM25-mined 0.756 (paired difference against in-batch +0.004 to +0.016), bge-mined 0.757 (+0.005 to +0.018). Unlike the sibling cross-encoder run, the bi-encoder keeps its in-batch negatives, so the mined one is an addition, not a replacement.
  3. The false-negative filter took the gain away: 0.748, against in-batch 0.746. It removed 42.1% of the top-10 candidates and pushed the first kept candidate to rank 3, so the negatives left were easier. Whether the removed abstracts were truly relevant needs new labels; on this set, keeping them helped.
  4. At a fixed number of epochs, smaller batches won: batch 8 0.760 (228 steps), 32 0.746 (56 steps), 128 0.732 (14 steps). With 919 pairs a bigger batch means far fewer updates, and that dominates; recipes like BGE's 19,200 train on millions of pairs, and this run cannot test that regime.
  5. No forgetting: every arm also gains +0.009 to +0.014 on NFCorpus, a domain it never saw.
  6. The noise floor: seeds move an arm's mean by at most 0.005, less than the effects in 1, 2 and 4; the filtered arm's +0.002 over in-batch is inside it. The test set adds a paired interval of about ±0.008 for differences between arms.
lab_note: What to watch. Training spreads the whole space: with filtered dense negatives the mean cosine of a claim to the random abstracts falls from 0.564 to 0.246, and to its own labelled abstract from 0.741 to 0.619. Absolute cosines fall; what retrieval needs is the gap between the labelled abstract and everything else. On these 12 claims the labelled abstract wins before training for 7 and after for 6: a sample this small does not show the gain that the 300-claim nDCG@10 measures (the chart above), which is why this view is for seeing the mechanism and the chart for judging it. measured here
